title: Pride and humility
hookLine: pride, the root sin, is cured by humility, seeing yourself truly

cards: Naaman is a great general, honored by his king, and he has leprosy. A captive girl from Israel, a servant in his house, tells his wife there's a prophet back home who could heal him.
So Naaman arrives at Elisha's door with horses and chariots and gifts. Elisha doesn't even come out. He sends a messenger: go wash in the Jordan.
And Naaman storms off in a rage. He expected the prophet to come out, call on God, wave a hand over the spot. Our rivers back home are better than that one, he says.
He's about to go home unhealed, because the cure was too ordinary for him.

teach.b: Then his servants step in, and what they say is the whole lesson in one sentence: "My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?"
Naaman listens. He goes down to the river, does exactly as he was told, and his skin comes back like a little child's.
Notice who rescued him from his pride: a captive girl and his own servants, the people he least expected to need. Some Christian teachers treat pride as the root of the other sins.

teach.h: PRIDE IS THE BEGINNING OF SIN.
teach.b: The Book of Sirach, in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and among the King James Apocrypha, puts it plainly: "pride is the beginning of sin."
And Proverbs adds where it leads: "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." But here's what's easy to get wrong. The cure isn't thinking you're worthless.
Paul tells the Romans "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly." Soberly: not higher than the truth, and not lower either.
Humility, in this picture, is simply seeing yourself truly: gifted and limited, capable and in need of help. Pride can't ask for help, because asking admits a limit. Humility asks easily.

The letter of James puts it in one line: "God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." Some readers hear Naaman in it: the gift was there all along, waiting for him to stoop to the river.

how: Some Christian traditions name pride among the deadly sins and humility as its remedy, and practice humility through confession, accepting correction and help, and serving others.

o: thinking too highly of yourself, and seeing yourself truly
confidence in your work, and shyness around people
self-respect, and putting yourself down to please others

games.q: you're Naaman. you came with chariots and gifts, and the prophet sends a messenger to tell you to wash in a river. what do you do?
o: go home; the rivers at home are better.
listen to your servants, and go wash as you were told.
demand that the prophet come out to you.
games.why: he nearly leaves in a rage, but his servants talk him around, he washes, and his skin comes back like a little child's.

practice: Think of one thing you've been struggling with alone because asking felt like admitting something, a task at work, a repair, a heavy week, and name one person who could help, maybe someone you wouldn't expect, like Naaman's servants.
Picture asking them, in plain words. If you pray, you can ask God for help too.

wordCard.voice: Pride and humility. Pride, which some Christian teachers call the root of sin, thinks higher of itself than the truth. Humility sees itself truly, and so it can ask for help.

orig.note: Greek: lowliness of mind, humility; the word in Philippians 2:3.

carryVoice: Your line: see yourself truly. Not higher than the truth, and not lower. Until tomorrow.
